title: The Dooars Tea Estates: CTC, Gardens and Garden Lines
meta_description: A guide to Dooars tea gardens: how CTC tea is made, the plucking year, the Chota Nagpur families who work the gardens, garden walks and visiting etiquette.
summary: Tea gardens cover much of the Dooars between the Teesta and the Sankosh, almost all making CTC tea for strong, milky chai. The first opened in 1874; families from Chota Nagpur and the Nepal hills built and still work them. Walk garden roads at 7 am, ask before entering lines or factories, and come from March to November for plucking.

sections.heading: A landscape made by tea
paras: Drive east from Sevoke and within half an hour the Dooars turn into an ocean of clipped green bushes, waist-high and flat-topped, under tall shade trees planted in rows. Garden follows garden for more than 150 km, broken by rivers, forest and the towns that grew around them: Malbazar, Chalsa, Nagrakata, Banarhat, Birpara, Hasimara, Kalchini. Many of these towns carry the names of the gardens they served, and the railway that links them was built to carry tea.

The first Dooars garden opened at Gazaldoba in 1874, nine years after the British annexed the region from Bhutan. Planters leased forest land along the foothills, cleared it and planted tea, and within a few decades the gardens ran the length of the region. Today the Dooars and the Terai below Darjeeling produce a large share of India's tea, most of it sold at auction in Siliguri and Kolkata and drunk as chai across the country.

sections.heading: CTC: the tea in your chai
paras: Darjeeling's hill gardens make orthodox tea: whole leaves rolled and dried slowly to keep their delicate flavour. The Dooars gardens, on hot, wet plains, mostly make CTC, which stands for crush, tear, curl. After withering, the green leaf goes through rollers with sharp teeth that cut it into small pieces and roll them into tiny granules. Oxidation is quick, and the dried granules brew dark, strong and fast, which is exactly what you want for tea boiled with milk and sugar.
The difference explains why a kilo of Dooars CTC costs a fraction of a fine Darjeeling flush, and why the gardens here are larger, flatter and more mechanised than those in the hills.

sections.heading: The people who work the gardens
paras: Clearing forest and plucking tea needed far more workers than the thinly populated plain could supply. From the late 19th century, recruiters known as sardars brought families from the Chota Nagpur plateau, in present-day Jharkhand and western Odisha: Oraon, Munda, Kharia, Santal and other Adivasi peoples. Nepali families came down from the hills. They lived in the labour lines of each garden, rows of small houses that became villages, and their common language, Sadri, is still spoken across the Dooars.

Plucking is mostly done by women, who pick two leaves and a bud by hand and carry the leaf in baskets or bags to weighing points. Men do much of the pruning, spraying and factory work. Under the Plantations Labour Act of 1951 gardens must provide housing, medical care and other benefits, but wages have long been among the lowest in organised work in West Bengal, and they are a constant subject of negotiation and protest.

Hard times have hit hard here. In the early 2000s several gardens closed when their owners abandoned them, and families in those gardens faced hunger. Many young people now leave for work in Kerala, Bengaluru and the Gulf. The festivals of the garden lines, especially Karam in the month of Bhadra, with drumming and dancing around branches of the karam tree, remain the strongest link with Chota Nagpur.

sections.heading: The plucking year
paras: Tea bushes here rest in winter. From December to February gardens are pruned back to bare frames and plucking stops; the bushes look grey and the gardens quiet. With the first warmth and rain in March, new shoots appear and the first flush is plucked. Through the monsoon, from June to September, growth is fastest and plucking runs every week or so, with the largest crop of the year. Production tails off in October and November.

For visitors this means the gardens are greenest and busiest from April to October, which overlaps only partly with the safari season. March, April and October give you both: parks open and pluckers out on the slopes.

sections.heading: Visiting a garden: walks, factories and stays
paras: The simplest way to see a tea garden is to walk its roads early in the morning. Around 7 am, pluckers walk out to the sections, supervisors check the day's work and the light under the shade trees is soft and green. Garden roads are working roads; walk on them, not between the bushes, and step aside for tractors.

Factories are not tourist attractions in the Dooars. A few gardens allow visits when asked politely through a manager or a homestay host, usually in the morning and not on busy days; most do not. Hygiene rules mean you may not be allowed beyond a viewing point. Never walk into a factory or into the labour lines without permission.

Some gardens have opened old managers' bungalows or garden houses to guests, and homestays in garden villages such as Samsing let you sleep among the bushes. Samsing, at about 900 m in the first hills above Chalsa, is the easiest place to combine tea and forest, with Rocky Island on the Murti and Suntalekhola nearby.
list: Ask before photographing pluckers; many will agree, some will not, and both answers deserve respect.
Do not pick leaves or walk through sections; bushes are pruned to a precise table height.
Keep to garden roads, especially at dusk, when elephants and leopards move through the gardens.
Buy local CTC from garden outlets or town shops rather than roadside stalls with unlabelled packets.

sections.heading: Where to see the gardens
paras: Good stretches for garden roads and views lie along the Sevoke–Malbazar–Chalsa road, where the hills rise behind the gardens; around Chalsa and Metali on the way up to Samsing; on the road from Nagrakata to Banarhat; and around Birpara and Hasimara on the way to Jaldapara. The Dooars line train runs through gardens for long stretches between Oodlabari and Hasimara; take a day train and sit on the north side.

Small tea growers are part of the picture now. Since the 1990s thousands of farmers around Jalpaiguri, Malbazar and Siliguri have planted tea on their own fields and sell green leaf to factories that buy it in. These smallholdings look different from the big estates, with bushes running right up to village houses.

faqs.q: What kind of tea is grown in the Dooars?
faqs.a: Mostly CTC, crush, tear, curl, a method that cuts withered leaf into small granules that brew dark, strong and fast. It is the tea behind India's milky, sugary chai. A few gardens make some orthodox leaf, but the Dooars are a CTC region, unlike the orthodox hill gardens of Darjeeling.

faqs.q: Can we visit a tea factory in the Dooars?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but not as a matter of course. A few gardens allow short visits if you ask politely through the manager or a homestay host, usually in the morning; many do not, for hygiene and work reasons. Never walk into a factory or labour lines without permission.

faqs.q: When was tea first planted in the Dooars?
faqs.a: The first Dooars tea garden opened at Gazaldoba in 1874, nine years after the Treaty of Sinchula ended the Duar War and handed the region to British India. Gardens spread quickly along the foothills, and the Bengal Dooars Railway was built in the 1890s to carry the tea out.

faqs.q: Who works in the Dooars tea gardens?
faqs.a: Mostly descendants of Oraon, Munda, Kharia, Santal and other Adivasi families brought from the Chota Nagpur plateau from the late 19th century, along with Nepali families. Women do most of the plucking. Their common language is Sadri, and festivals such as Karam came with them from Chota Nagpur.

faqs.q: When is the plucking season in the Dooars?
faqs.a: Roughly March to November. Gardens are pruned and plucking stops from December to February. The first flush comes in March and April, the heaviest crop in the monsoon months, and production tails off in October and November. March, April and October combine plucking with open parks.

faqs.q: Where can we stay in a tea garden in the Dooars?
faqs.a: Samsing, a tea garden village at about 900 m above Chalsa, has homestays among the bushes for ₹1,200–1,800 per person with meals. Some gardens have opened old managers' bungalows to guests at higher prices. Ask about meals and access before booking, since gardens are working estates.

faqs.q: Is it okay to photograph tea pluckers?
faqs.a: Ask first, every time. Many pluckers will agree, some will not, and both answers deserve respect. Do not walk between bushes to get closer or interrupt work at weighing points. Photographs of garden roads, shade trees and the hills behind need no permission.

faqs.q: Can we buy Dooars tea to take home?
faqs.a: Yes. Shops in Malbazar, Birpara, Madarihat and Siliguri sell local CTC in sealed packets at modest prices, and some gardens sell from outlets. Avoid unlabelled loose tea at roadside stalls. For orthodox whole-leaf tea, Darjeeling and Mirik shops have more choice.

faqs.q: Are elephants found in tea gardens?
faqs.a: Yes, often. Elephants, leopards and gaur move through the gardens between forest patches, especially at dusk and night, and conflicts with workers are a real problem. Walk garden roads in daylight, keep away from drains and thick sections at dusk, and listen to local advice.
